I was driving yesterday afternoon in a hansom cab down one of the sloping streets into the Strand, reading one of my own admirable articles with continual pleasure, and still more continual surprise, when the horse fell forward, scrambled a moment on the scraping stones, staggered to his feet again, and went forward. The horses in my cabs often do this, and I have learnt to enjoy my own articles at any angle of the vehicle. So I did not see anything at all odd about the way the horse went on again. But I saw it suddenly in the faces of all the people on the pavement. They were all turned towards me, and they were all struck with fear suddenly, as with a white flame out of the sky. And one man half ran out into the road with a movement of the elbow as if warding off a blow, and tried to stop the horse. Then I knew that the reins were lost, and the next moment the horse was like a living thunder-bolt. I try to describe things exactly as they seemed to me; many details I may have missed or mis-stated; many details may have, so to speak, gone mad in the race down the road. I remember that I once called one of my experiences narrated in this paper “A Fragment of Fact.” This is, at any rate, a fragment of fact. No fact could possibly be more fragmentary than the sort of fact that I expected to be at the bottom of that street.

.....

I believe in preaching to the converted; for I have generally found that the converted do not understand their own religion. Thus I have always urged in this paper that democracy has a deeper meaning than democrats understand; that is, that common and popular things, proverbs, and ordinary sayings always have something in them unrealised by most who repeat them. Here is one. We have all heard about the man who is in momentary danger, and who sees the whole of his life pass before him in a moment. In the cold, literal, and common sense of words, this is obviously a thundering lie. Nobody can pretend that in an accident or a mortal crisis he elaborately remembered all the tickets he had ever taken to Wimbledon, or all the times that he had ever passed the brown bread and butter.

But in those few moments, while my cab was tearing towards the traffic of the Strand, I discovered that there is a truth behind this phrase, as there is behind all popular phrases. I did really have, in that short and shrieking period, a rapid succession of a number of fundamental points of view. I had, so to speak, about five religions in almost as many seconds. My first religion was pure Paganism, which among sincere men is more shortly described as extreme fear. Then there succeeded a state of mind which is quite real, but for which no proper name has ever been found. The ancients called it Stoicism, and I think it must be what some German lunatics mean (if they mean anything) when they talk about Pessimism. It was an empty and open acceptance of the thing that happens—as if one had got beyond the value of it. And then, curiously enough, came a very strong contrary feeling—that things mattered very much indeed, and yet that they were something more than tragic. It was a feeling, not that life was unimportant, but that life was much too important ever to be anything but life. I hope that this was Christianity. At any rate, it occurred at the moment when we went crash into the omnibus.

message.content:
As I drove along in a hansom cab yesterday afternoon, descending one of the inclined streets leading into the Strand, I found myself engrossed in one of my own articles, deriving immense enjoyment and a sense of astonishment from it. Suddenly, the horse stumbled, fell forward, struggled momentarily on the rough stones, then regained its footing and continued on. This kind of behavior from the horses in my cabs was not unusual, and I had grown accustomed to appreciating my articles regardless of the motion of the vehicle. Therefore, I didn't initially find anything peculiar about the horse's recovery. However, the expressions of fear etched on the faces of those on the sidewalk caught my attention. They all turned toward me, their features marked by terror, as if struck by a sudden lightning bolt. One man even rushed into the street, raising his arm as if to deflect an impending blow, attempting to halt the horse. At that moment, I realized the reins had slipped from my grasp, and in the next instant, the horse became a living projectile. I strive to recount events as accurately as possible; yet, I recognize that many details might have escaped my notice or become distorted in the rush down the road. In a previous account, I referred to one of my experiences in this paper as “A Fragment of Fact.” This situation, too, is undoubtedly a fragment of reality, though the nature of the facts I anticipated at the end of that street was decidedly chaotic.

I have always been an advocate of speaking to those who are already inclined to agree; my experiences suggest that those who hold certain beliefs often lack a true understanding of their own convictions. Thus, I have consistently maintained in this paper that democracy encompasses a more profound significance than many of its proponents grasp. Common phrases and widely held beliefs often encapsulate deeper truths that go unrecognized by those who frequently repeat them. Consider the well-known notion of a person facing imminent peril who suddenly experiences their entire life flashing before their eyes. Taken literally, this idea seems utterly absurd. No one can convincingly claim that during a life-threatening incident, they meticulously recalled every ticket they ever purchased to Wimbledon or all the times they shared brown bread and butter.

Yet, in the fleeting moments while my cab raced toward the bustling traffic of the Strand, I discerned an underlying truth behind this expression, as is the case with many popular sayings. During that brief, frantic interval, a rapid succession of fundamental perspectives surged through my mind. In what felt like merely seconds, I encountered what could be described as five distinct belief systems. Initially, I experienced pure Paganism, which could be succinctly characterized as intense fear. This was swiftly followed by a mindset that, while real, lacks a precise name. The ancients might have referred to it as Stoicism, and it seems akin to what some German thinkers, if they have any coherent ideas at all, describe as Pessimism. It represented an empty acceptance of whatever unfolds, as if the significance of it had been transcended. Then, rather interestingly, I was struck by a contrasting realization—that life indeed mattered immensely, yet there was something beyond tragedy in its essence. This sensation wasn’t that existence was trivial; rather, it was a recognition that life was far too significant to ever be reduced to mere existence. I hope to attribute this feeling to Christianity, as it emerged just as we collided with the omnibus.
